entries.text: A command is no longer lost, or applied twice, when the connection drops on its way. `RoomClient` names itself when it connects and numbers its commands; the room remembers how far it got with them, in the same write as the state, and says so when the client is back (protocol version 5: `c`, `from` and `refused` in `welcome`). The client settles the commands the room handled and sends the others again, so the promise from `send()` resolves or rejects as if the connection had held, through a deploy or a restart of the room too. A command waits for at most `keepCommandsMs`, ten seconds by default. It costs no rows beyond the saves a room makes anyway, but for one when a page is loaded again while its player holds a seat. Lockstep rooms and the Godot and Unity clients do not take part yet, and a room opts out with `rememberCommands = false`. See [When the connection drops](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/guide/client#when-the-connection-drops).

A ticking room can simulate more often than it sends. Set `patchRate` below `tickRate` (60 ticks and 20 patches a second, say) and the room runs every tick but sends each player what changed only that many times a second, in one patch for the ticks in between. What a patch costs, `view()` for every player, the comparison and the bytes, is paid that much less often. A command is acknowledged with the patch that shows it, and messages sent from `onTick` wait for it too; nothing waits when the simulation stops. `RoomClient.patchRate` says how often patches come, `BufferedInterpolator` keeps one patch more of a delay by itself, and an `Interpolator` should glide for `1000 / room.patchRate` ms. The Godot and Unity clients work with such a room but do not read the rate yet. See [Sending less often than you simulate](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/guide/state-sync#sending-less-often-than-you-simulate).

`parseWith(schema, raw)` checks a command against a schema from any library that implements Standard Schema, such as Zod, Valibot or ArkType: `protected parseCommand(raw: unknown) { return parseWith(Command, raw); }`. The room gets what the schema gives back, and what does not fit is refused with the first thing the schema found wrong and where, as `invalid_command: Expected number (at x)`. It works for `parseInput` in a lockstep room too, and Tickflare depends on none of the libraries. See [Checking commands with a schema](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/guide/rooms#checking-commands-with-a-schema).

A lockstep desync now says whose simulations differed and where. `desync.players` in the view names the two players whose hashes differed, and `onDesync` gets them, on the server as `onDesync(turn, players)` and in `LockstepClient` as `onDesync(turn, desync)`. With a simulation that has `save`, the two clients then send the room what they had saved at that turn, and the room puts the first eight places where the two differ in `desync.differs`, as a path into what `save` returns and the two values: `units.tank.x`, `"14"` and `"14.5"`. `onDesyncExplained` runs on the server and in every client when it is known. A client with a `hash` of its own takes part with `explainDesyncs: true`. `differences(a, b)`, the comparison itself, is exported for tests of your own. See [Finding a desync](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/guide/lockstep#finding-a-desync).

A ticking room can keep the state of its last ticks and judge a command by the one its player was looking at, which is what lag compensation needs. Set `historyTicks` (12 at 60 ticks a second is 200 ms) and `stateAt(tick)` returns the state as that tick left it, or `undefined` when the room does not have it. On the client, `BufferedInterpolator.drawnTick()` says which tick is on screen, to send with the command. Keeping the ticks costs no work in a tick, only memory, and `historyTicks` is also as far back as a client can claim to have seen. See [Judging a command by what its player saw](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/guide/state-sync#judging-a-command-by-what-its-player-saw).

Spectators: connections that watch a room without a seat in it. Set `maxSpectators` on the room and connect with `new RoomClient(url, { spectate: true })`. A spectator is sent the room's `spectatorView()`, kept up to date like a player's view, with who is here and what the room broadcasts; they are not among `players`, no seat hook runs for them, and what they send is refused. `spectatorDelayMs` keeps them that far behind the players, in everything, so that watching is no help to someone who plays. `onSpectate(player)` decides who may watch, and a room with a `view()` of its own takes no spectators until it has a `spectatorView()`. Not for lockstep rooms, and not yet in the Godot and Unity clients. On the wire a spectator asks with `spectate=1` and is answered with a `spectating` frame in place of `welcome`; a gateway of your own should hand such a request to the room under `x-tickflare-spectator`, as `routeToRoom` does. See [Spectators](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/guide/spectators).

`RoomClient.send()` and `leave()` wait for a connection instead of rejecting with `not_connected` at once. A command sent while the client is connecting, the first time or again, is held, shows in `unconfirmed`, and goes out when the room answers; it rejects with `not_connected` only after `keepCommandsMs` without one. A command that was in flight when the connection dropped rejects with `disconnected` only when the client could not find out what became of it, and no longer at the moment of the drop. Pass `keepCommandsMs: 0` to keep the old behaviour.

Rooms tell clients their clock: protocol version 4 adds the clock to `welcome` and a `clock` frame, and `RoomClient.serverTick()` estimates the tick the room is on right now, using `RoomClient.rtt`, the smoothed round trip. Clients of version 3 and earlier, including the Godot and Unity clients, are sent nothing new. See [The room's clock](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/reference/protocol#the-room-s-clock).

`BufferedInterpolator` draws what moves at the room's own pace: it keeps the last few states of each thing by tick and draws a moment a little behind the room's clock, with a delay that adapts to the jitter it measures. When updates stop it carries things on at their last speed for a few ticks, it draws a jump as one (`snap(id)` or `snapDistance`), and it turns angles the short way round. It has the same `update` and `at` as `Interpolator`, which stays for a player's own predicted moves. See [Drawing at the room's pace](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/guide/state-sync#drawing-at-the-room-s-pace).

A ticking room keeps to a fixed clock. When it wakes late, because a tick or an event took long or the machine was busy, it runs every tick that has come due since, each with the same `dt`, and sends one patch for them all, so a room that falls behind now and then gets back on time instead of slowing the game down. After a stall of more than `maxCatchUpTicks` ticks (5 by default) it runs that many and lets the rest go. `onTick` can therefore run several times back to back; set `maxCatchUpTicks = 1` to keep the old behaviour. See [Keeping time](https://tickflare.gridpaper.dev/guide/state-sync#keeping-time).
